articles.title: Roman lifts off on a mission to survey the infrared sky
articles.description:
Image:
			
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA, at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST/ 13:26 CEST on 30 August 2026. With the successful launch, Roman began its mission to survey the sky in visible to near-infrared light to help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter. The telescope will also investigate the true diversity of exoplanets in our galaxy.
Roman is a NASA-led mission to which the European Space Agency (ESA) contributed star trackers, batteries, and detectors for the coronagraph instrument. ESA will also provide communications support through its deep-space ground station network, and enable data download using its new 35-metre antenna in New Norcia, Australia.
“I warmly congratulate our colleagues at NASA on the successful launch of Roman,” says Carole Mundell, ESA’s Director of Science. “ESA is proud to have provided essential hardware and to continue supporting Roman’s ambitious scientific goals. Together, we are opening new windows on the cosmos.”
Like ESA’s Euclid space telescope, Roman will enable astronomers to study the Universe in unprecedented detail. It is equipped with a primary mirror of 2.4 m and two instruments: the Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration.
With its panoramic view of the sky, crisp infrared vision and quick re-orientation skills, Roman will perform fast and efficient surveys of a large area of the sky. By doing so, it will map clustering of galaxies over time and space and also study the light coming from thousands of distant type Ia supernovas which will help astronomers trace the expansion of the Universe.
“Roman should provide our clearest picture yet of whether dark energy is truly constant or whether it evolves over cosmic time – either outcome would have profound implications for our understanding of the Universe. I'm also excited by Roman's exoplanet census, which will discover thousands of new worlds, including cold planets and free-floating planets that have remained largely beyond our reach until now,” says Bethan James, ESA’s Roman Project Scientist. “Perhaps what excites me most is the unexpected. With its unprecedented combination of depth, area, and image quality, Roman has every opportunity to surprise us.”
After launch, Roman is on a steady course to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), nearly 1.5 million km away from Earth. This location allows the telescope to have an unobstructed view of a wide area of the sky, almost 12%. Like ESA’s Euclid and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, Roman will move in a wider orbit around the L2 point – much larger than the Moon’s orbit around Earth.
In the next three months following launch, the Roman team will conduct a carefully orchestrated series of deployments, calibrations, and tests. Once the commissioning period is complete, the mission will begin its science operations, starting with the first science image release. Roman will spend at least five years scanning the infrared sky and is designed to work in space for another five years.
[Image description: A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on board is seen transiting the Sun during launch from Launch Complex 39A, on Sunday 30 August 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, US.]
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope successfully launches aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket to conduct an infrared survey of the cosmos.

articles.title: Watch live: BepiColombo begins its arrival at Mercury
articles.description:
After eight years, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission is about to enter its Mercury Arrival Phase. On 3 September 2026, ESA’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from BepiColombo’s two science orbiters – the first major step in one of the most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.  
The European Space Agency (ESA) will livestream the critical milestone from 13:45 CEST. Tune in and witness the first step of one of the most complex phases of the mission, live from ESA mission control.  
Join ESA's livestream on YouTube here!
articles.summary: The ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission is beginning its arrival phase at Mercury after eight years of travel, marking a major milestone in planetary exploration.

articles.title: Scientists observe Einstein’s gravity in the quantum world for the first time
articles.description: Physicists have directly observed a long-predicted quantum effect of gravity, putting one of Einstein’s foundational ideas to a striking new test. Using ultracold atoms, researchers split an atom’s quantum wave so that one part was held in place while the other fell freely under gravity, then reunited the two to measure the tiny difference that emerged.
articles.summary: Physicists have directly observed a quantum effect of gravity predicted by Einstein's theories, confirming foundational ideas about gravity at the quantum scale.

articles.title: On this day in space! Sept. 11, 1985: The International Cometary Explorer makes 1st comet flyby in history for NASA and Europe
articles.description: On Sept. 11, 1985, the International Cometary Explorer, or "ICE," became the first spacecraft to fly by a comet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.summary: On September 11, 1985, the International Cometary Explorer became the first spacecraft to fly by a comet, marking a historic milestone for NASA and European space agencies.

articles.title: Is it a planet or a moon? Scientists discover a strange Jupiter-sized world orbiting a brown dwarf in a never-before-seen cosmic system
articles.description: Astronomers found a massive object orbiting a brown dwarf star. This discovery challenges existing definitions of planets and moons. The unusual system features a nested orbital arrangement unlike our solar system. Scientists are debating the object's classif…
articles.summary: Astronomers discovered a Jupiter-sized object orbiting a brown dwarf in an unprecedented system, challenging conventional definitions of planets and moons.

articles.title: NASA’s Chandra Spots Galactic Gem
articles.description: Two galaxies merge at a furious rate in this Aug. 25, 2026, image of the II Zw 096 system. This and several other images of both visually and scientifically interesting galaxies were released by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and other telescopes. Chandra X-ray data (magenta) pinpoint powerful black hole activity and hot gas, while optical […]
articles.summary: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory captures a stunning image of the II Zw 096 system showing two galaxies merging at an intense rate.

articles.title: NASA Boosts Open Science, Data Sharing with Artemis Accords
articles.description: The science from every Moon rock sample, lunar dataset, and discovery produced through NASA’s Artemis program will be shared by the agency with the global scientific community. That commitment is upheld by all 71 countries that have signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for safe and transparent civil space exploration. NASA put those […]
articles.summary: NASA commits to open science and data sharing under the Artemis Accords, ensuring all lunar discoveries and samples are accessible to the global scientific community.

articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: BepiColombo successfully completes Mercury Transfer Module separation, a critical milestone in the European-Japanese mission to explore Mercury.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn’s famous hexagon at its northern pole, but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon develop on the iconic gas giant.
articles.summary: Hubble observations reveal a remarkable 10-sided atmospheric wave structure evolving around Saturn's south pole, a surprising geometric phenomenon.

articles.title: Dense Galaxies Are Carving Out A Bubble in the Early Universe
articles.description: Light could only travel freely in the Universe after cosmic reionization. Before that, neutral hydrogen stopped photons from travelling. The JWST has found evidence of an overdensity of galaxies carving out a bubble of reionization. Is this how it all started?
articles.summary: Dense galaxies in the early universe are creating bubbles that allow light to travel freely during cosmic reionization, revealing insights into the universe's first epochs.

articles.title: How Big Can The Universe's First Starbursts Get?
articles.description: As our telescopes have improved and we’ve been able to peer farther back in time, we’ve begun finding more fascinating features of the universe. But one thing we definitely haven’t found yet is Population III (Pop III) stars. These were the earliest stars in the universe, formed completely from pristine hydrogen and helium, with no “metals” (i.e. elements heavier than those two) polluting their processes. They are also theorized to be absolutely massive, and “die with passion” as Bill Wurtz once put it in a famous YouTube video. A new paper, available in pre-print form on arXiv by Tae Bong Jeon from the Cosmic Frontier Center at the University of Texas at Austin, looks at just how massive those starbursts could be, and whether the James Webb Space Telescope could detect one.
articles.summary: Improved telescopes are revealing fascinating insights into the scale and properties of the universe's first starburst galaxies, pushing back the boundaries of cosmic observation.

articles.title: NASA's Next Great Observatory Could Spot Oceans on Distant Worlds
articles.description: We’ve found over 5,500 exoplanets so far. Dozens of them have been in the habitable zone of their parent stars, where, at least in theory, they could host an ocean. But we’ve never definitively found a liquid ocean on another planet. A new paper from researchers Eleanor Cornish and Tyler Robinson of the University of Arizona, available in pre-print on arXiv and submitted to the Astrophysical Journal, looks at a unique way we might be able to find one - by looking for its “glint”.
articles.summary: NASA's next-generation observatory could detect oceans on distant exoplanets, advancing our ability to search for potentially habitable worlds beyond our solar system.

articles.title: eROSITA's Second Data Release Catalog Delivering the Most Comprehensive High-Energy Census of the Cosmos to Date
articles.description: The eROSITA Consortium has issued the survey's second data release (DR2), nearly doubling the previously known eROSITA X-ray sources to two million.
articles.summary: eROSITA's second data release provides the most comprehensive high-energy census of the cosmos, nearly doubling previously known X-ray sources across the universe.

articles.title: Unexplained Gamma-Rays from the Galactic Center Could be from Self-Annihilating Dark Matter
articles.description: Over a decade ago, the Fermi satellite detected an excess of gamma-ray emissions in the galactic center. Potential explanations included Sgr. A*, the Milky Way's SMBH, pulsars, and even self-annihilating dark matter. There's no clear answer yet, since the region is so difficult to observe. But recent research shows that dark matter can't be ruled out.
articles.summary: Unexplained gamma-ray emissions from the galactic center detected by Fermi may be evidence of self-annihilating dark matter, offering potential insights into dark matter's nature.

articles.title: A New Surface Atlas of Phobos Will Help JAXA's MMX Mission Collect its Samples
articles.description: JAXA's Martian Moon eXploration (MMX) will be on its way to Mars and Phobos next month. It will collect samples from Phobos and return them to Earth. A new morphodynamic atlas of the small moon will help scientists collect and understand the samples.
articles.summary: A new surface atlas of Phobos will guide JAXA's Martian Moon eXploration mission in collecting samples from the Martian moon next month.

articles.title: Scientists discover a strange new form of ice that could help explain the interiors of Neptune and Uranus
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that there is ice deep inside planets like Neptune and Uranus and want to find out what form it takes and how it behaves. They cannot dig for it and transport it all the way back to Earth, so they do the next best thing: recreate those extreme conditions in the lab.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange new form of ice that may exist in the interiors of Neptune and Uranus, deepening our understanding of ice giant composition.

articles.title: Release of open AI model trained on 17 years of lunar data maps ice, craters and volcanoes
articles.description: NASA is bringing artificial intelligence to the study of the moon, helping researchers transform how they analyze its surface. In an ongoing collaboration with IBM Research and several academic institutions, NASA has launched the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model, one of the first open-source AI models built specifically for lunar science. The model, trained primarily on data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), is hosted publicly on Hugging Face for anyone to use, with the complete codebase available on GitHub for testing and experimentation.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA has released an open AI model trained on 17 years of lunar data that maps ice, craters, and volcanoes, transforming lunar surface analysis research.

articles.title: Continuous video of black hole radio observations challenges shock wave theory
articles.description: For years, scientists have relied primarily on radio imaging from techniques like very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) to study jets from the active galactic nuclei of supermassive black holes. This allows for the detection of broad, unresolved features, called components, moving at what appear to be faster-than-light speeds. However, traditional imaging has poor resolution and treats each observation as a separate snapshot in time, limiting information about how the features move.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Continuous video observations of black hole radio emissions challenge existing shock wave theory, providing new insights into black hole behavior and astrophysical processes.

articles.title: Physicists just found a tiny glitch in time itself
articles.description: Unconventional quantum theories may imply that time itself has a tiny fundamental uncertainty, placing an ultimate limit on how precisely any clock could measure it. The effect is far beyond current detection, but it could reveal a hidden connection between quantum mechanics, gravity, and spacetime.
articles.summary: Physicists have discovered that quantum theories suggest time itself has fundamental uncertainty at the most basic level, revealing an ultimate limit to temporal precision.

articles.title: The Moon may have formed intact just hours after a giant collision
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the Moon-forming collision may have depended heavily on how hot and physically strong early Earth and Theia were. New simulations found that some impacts create the familiar disk of debris that later becomes the Moon, while others can produce an intact Moon in only about five hours. The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the enormous collision could be modeled as if both worlds behaved mostly like fluids.
articles.summary: New research suggests the Moon may have formed intact just hours after the giant collision that created it, challenging previous formation timelines.

articles.title: Astronomers detect ancient hydrogen signal that could help map the Universe
articles.description: Astronomers have detected an exceptionally faint hydrogen radio signal from billions of light-years away using South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. Instead of finding galaxies one at a time, the technique measures their combined hydrogen glow across enormous stretches of space. The successful detection shows that astronomers may soon be able to create much larger 3D maps of the Universe.
articles.summary: Astronomers have detected an exceptionally faint ancient hydrogen radio signal from billions of light-years away, opening new possibilities for mapping the universe.

articles.title: Four amateur astronomers using a telescope in Chile’s Atacama desert found a comet on 13 January 2026, 81 days before it would graze past the Sun. Nobody alive had seen its previous pass, because the orbit it travels on brings it back only about every 1,900 years.
articles.description:
A glimpse of a celestial wanderer that last visited during the Middle Ages—caught not by professional observatories, but by four amateurs with a telescope and patience.
The post Four amateur astronomers using a telescope in Chile’s Atacama desert found a come…
articles.summary: Amateur astronomers in Chile's Atacama desert discovered a rare comet on January 13, 2026, with an orbital period of approximately 1,900 years—a celestial visitor unseen since the Middle Ages.

articles.title: Icy Exocomets Around a Distant Star Help Explain Earth's Water
articles.description: Did icy comets deliver water to the young Earth? That idea won't go away. Now, astronomers at Lund University in Sweden have found evidence of exocomets orbiting a young star named PDS 70. The observations suggest that these comets are delivering water to tha…
articles.summary: Astronomers at Lund University discovered icy exocomets orbiting a distant star, providing new insights into how cometary delivery may have brought water to young Earth.

articles.title: Astronomy Picture of the Day - Hubble: Decagon Around Saturn's South Pole
articles.description: Explanation: Why are Saturn’s poles geometric? Saturn’s North Pole has been known to be surrounded by a hexagonal (6 sides) cloud since discovery in 1987 in data taken by NASA’s Voyager spacecrafts, which quickly flew past the ringed world in the early 1980s.…
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope has revealed a geometric 10-sided atmospheric pattern circling Saturn's south pole, adding to the mystery of Saturn's geometric polar structures.

articles.title: Rubin Observatory Peers Deep Into the Famous COSMOS Field
articles.description: A new image from NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory offers a spectacularly deep view into a famous region of sky known as the COSMOS field.
articles.summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory has captured a spectacular deep-field image of the famous COSMOS region, advancing our understanding of the distant universe.

articles.title: In 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars from a radio telescope in Puerto Rico, aimed at a cluster 25,000 light-years away
articles.description:
On 16 November 1974, the Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico transmitted humanity's first deliberate interstellar message toward the M13 star cluster — a 1,679-bit binary picture that will not arrive for 25,000 years.
The post In 1974, humans sent their fi…
articles.summary: On November 16, 1974, the Arecibo radio telescope transmitted humanity's first deliberate interstellar message toward a star cluster 25,000 light-years away.

articles.title: Astronomers Hear the Faint Whispers of Cosmic Hydrogen from the Distant Past.
articles.description: Astronomers have directly detected an extremely faint radio signal from hydrogen gas billions of light years away, demonstrating a powerful new way to map the Universe.
articles.summary: Astronomers have directly detected an extremely faint radio signal from hydrogen gas billions of light-years away, revealing the distant cosmic past.

articles.title: Help Refine Data from Space Telescopes with Artifact InSPECtor
articles.description: How do scientists studying space with data from a telescope hundreds of thousands of miles away know that what they are seeing is real? A new NASA project, Artifact InSPECtor, invites you to find out – and by doing so, to help missions like Euclid and NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope answer fundamental […]
articles.summary: Scientists use innovative artifact detection methods to refine and validate data from distant space telescopes, improving the reliability of astronomical observations.

articles.title: NASA Answers President’s Call to Establish United States Space Academy
articles.description: Less than two weeks after an Executive Order was signed to create the first United States Space Academy, NASA-led work is in full swing to make the academy a reality and shape the future of America’s aerospace workforce and leadership. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman chaired the first Presidential Commission on the United States Space Academy […]
articles.summary: NASA leads efforts to establish the United States Space Academy, advancing the next generation of space professionals and explorers.

articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: Watch the complete replay of BepiColombo's Mercury arrival livestream as the ESA-JAXA mission reaches a major mission milestone.
